en: Śākti Śānti Oṃ Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Bhagavatī Vajravārāhī!
Oṃ!
This Fortune of the Fully Awakened One has arisen from the ornament of the ocean of bliss; she is endowed with all forms of virtue and destroys the mass of darkness that is the world’s evil.
May the Blessed Lady Durgā— who is the treasury of the knowledge of the stars, the steadfastness of the treasury of memory, and the wisdom of the treasury of intelligence—
protect the three worlds from misfortune.
Having paid homage to the line of pollen from the lotus feet of Śrīvatradevī and to the feet of the Guru;
Śrīsaṃvara is the concealed bodhicitta, the praised state consisting of the two feet of wisdom and compassion.
By the monk Jñānendra, who dwells in the bliss of prostrating at the two feet of Vajradevī, Candra Vasuśarman.
The sādhana of Vajravārāhī for one's own benefit is here briefly analyzed.
The mind is ever eager for conceptualization toward one who bestows well-spoken words.
Therefore, with faith as my primary motive, this has been composed by me, whose intellect is dull and very limited.
This must be done; the great people should not look for fault in me.

5. The venerable teacher Śūnyatāsamādhivajrapāda, desiring to compose the *Sādhana* of the illustrious Vajradevī, first composed two verses intended as a benediction by means of manifesting the essential nature and qualities of the Blessed Lady.

Oṃ! Homage to the illustrious Vajravārāhī, whose splendor is radiant with the flickering of lightning stirred by the wind from the wheel of the nether regions; she who has incinerated the three cities of the Asuras, is honored by the three worlds, and is drenched in a stream of nectar.

May Vārāhikā protect you—she who is permeated by the essence of the Buddha’s gnosis, free from defilement, bestowing a mass of her own bliss, and devoid of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.
She is Vārāhī because she brings forth the excellent mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*); [the root] *hi* means "to go.
With the prefix *ā*, it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*);
the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs according to the rule governing words such as *pṛṣodara*.
The meaning is that she follows the Blessed One who resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Since the bodhicitta and the Blessed One are non-different, what is the Blessed Lady like?
She is "risen," meaning she has gone upward; from where? From the *talacakra*, which is the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
Shaken by the wind— that is, agitated by the vital breath known as *apāna*—
she is radiant like a flash of lightning; she is both passionate and stainless, having burnt away the three impurities.
She by whom the three *ālis* have been burned.

By the word *āli*, the wheel (*cakra*) is denoted—namely, those called the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *mahāsukhakāya*. They are "burned" because of the departure of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
She is honored by the three worlds.
She who is honored and worshipped by the three classes of gods belonging to the realms of desire and form is thus described.

Alternatively, the three wheels themselves are drenched by a stream of nectar (*pīyūṣa*). "Nectar" refers to the bodhicitta; it is "drenched," meaning bathed. External worship is also performed with water and other substances;
here, however, the very stream of bodhicitta constitutes the bathing with water.
She is permeated by the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom.

The Buddha’s wisdom is free from conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence; that very wisdom is the "essence" (rasa), and she is "permeated" (āvilā) by it, because the Blessed Lady consists of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).
For this very reason, she is stainless (*vikaluṣā*).
The emission of the *bodhicitta* is designated as "defilement" (*kaluṣa*).

For this very reason, detachment (*virāga*) arises. According to the scriptural teaching: "From the occurrence of emission comes the birth of detachment; from the birth of detachment comes the arising of suffering"—that which brings about cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) through karma is itself suffering.
It arises precisely from death.
And thus it is said:
"There is no sin greater than lack of dispassion, and no merit greater than happiness."
"Bestowing a mass of one's own bliss.
A mass of bliss is a "svānandasandoha"; she gives that well (*suṣṭhu*)—this is the sense, with the words "to all people" being understood as the ellipsis.
It is devoid of the investigation into existence and non-existence.
"Existence" is the grasping at permanence, and "non-existence" is the grasping at annihilation; it is devoid of the investigation into those two because it is completely filled with supreme bliss.

May Vārāhikā—who resides within the solar orb of emanation, who blazes with the brilliance of kindled fire, who is surrounded by the phonemes beginning with *ka*, who is like a subtle lotus-thread, who pierces through the three wheels (*cakras*), and who consumes the assembly of Buddhas through wisdom—may she, the blissful one moving gracefully upward, manifest within your hearts.
"Situated within the solar mandala of the emanation lotus" means she is situated within the solar mandala of the emanation wheel.
Enveloped by the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth, this Vajravārāhī is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*); and the Blessed Lady has pervaded the external world by means of that wisdom.
Blazing with a fire that is intensely radiant,
because her form is exceedingly luminous and because she burns away all the darkness of evil.

"Amṛtasavā" means she whose bath (*sava*) is with nectar (*amṛta*), which is the bodhicitta. "Sūkṣmābjasūtropamā" means she whose likeness is to a subtle lotus-fiber; that is, her likeness is to a subtle lotus-fiber, a lotus-stalk fiber.
This is because she has the nature of *avadhūtī* and because she indicates the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-jñāna*).
"She burns the assembly of the Vidyās and Buddhas" means she burns the union of the Vidyās—Locanā and the others, who have the nature of earth and so forth—and the Buddhas—Vairocana and the others.
It causes entry into the object of focus;
and thus it is said in the Hevajra [Tantra]:
“The Caṇḍālī, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas; she burns Locanā and the others, and from her, the Moon gives birth to the [five] Dahrarohas.
Thus, this Blessed Lady is Caṇḍālī in her own form.
She pierces the three wheels by ascending through the wheel of dharma, the wheel of enjoyment, and the wheel of great bliss.

For this very reason, Lalitā is accompanied by bliss because she arises from the excellence of all aspects; she is "upward-moving" because she constantly proceeds upward toward the mandala of great bliss.
Having prostrated with my head before Vajravārāhī, the Vajrayoginī who is preceded by the Vajra,
I shall explain for my own recollection the perfect accomplishment of the knowledge of reality.
Its intrinsic nature is reality (*tattva*).
Because it is stated that its characteristic is non-arising, its reality is non-arising.
Its knowledge is correct awakening; having prostrated to Vajravārāhī—meaning she who is preceded by the *vajra*, namely Vārāhī—I shall describe her correct faith.
Vajrayoginī is the non-apprehension wisdom (*anupalambhajñāna*) of the vajra.
She is so called because she possesses yoga together with that. "With the head" means with the uppermost part of the body.
"For what purpose shall I speak? For my own remembrance; that is to say, for the sake of recollecting myself.
This is precisely the avoidance of arrogance on the part of the excellent teacher.
The wise man, mindful and desiring a favorable location, should enter while holding his Lord upon his shoulder.
There, having sat upon a comfortable seat, one should contemplate purification.
This is the connection with Diti.
The meaning is that one should meditate upon emptiness.

According to the principle that "the purity of all things is considered to be suchness (*tathatā*)," the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely the abandonment of the entire mass of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) accumulated since beginningless time. Having entered a secluded place devoid of people, one sits alone for the sake of concentrating the mind. A secluded place may be of any kind, yet it does not serve to concentrate the mind unless it is agreeable to the mind; therefore, he says "agreeable to the mind" (*mano'nukūla*), where stability of mind occurs. Having made one's seat there and sat down—the seat being not merely ordinary but one that causes happiness—he specifies it as "delicate" (*sukumāra*) and "soft" (*komala*). What is its specific characteristic? It is "marked by the Lord" (*nāthāṅkaka*); the "Lord" (*nātha*) is one’s own Guru, and that by which the head is marked or characterized is "marked by the Lord. Alternatively, it refers to one whose head is marked by Vairocana, for only the wise (*sudhī*, *paṇḍita*) have authority over such a matter. Now, the specific meaning is explained: "secluded" (*vijana*) means where the perception of people has departed; thus, "secluded" is a characteristic of the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Therefore, it is "agreeable to the mind" because the one-pointedness of the mind is possible only in Great Bliss. It is a "place" (*sthāna*) because the world abides therein, according to the saying, "The world consists of all happiness. It is "marked by the Lord" (*nāthāṅkaka*): the "Lord" is the Vajra-Guru, his "mark" (*aṅka*) is the sign, and the "fourth moment" (*caturthakṣaṇa*) is the "bliss" (*kaṃ*) therein; thus, he is "marked by the Lord. For this very reason, he is "wise" (*sudhī*). Furthermore, that [wisdom] depends upon a cause; he states that cause: having sat upon a "delicate seat" (*sukumāram āsanam*). By "delicate," he indicates one endowed with the prime of youth, for it is only there that the arising of Great Bliss is possible. "Having sat" means having entered into union (*dvaṃdva*). Herein it is said:

If even that bliss (*sukha*) is dependent upon causes, how can it be called "Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*)? That which is subject to causes is impermanent; how then can it be bliss? Furthermore, for that which is impermanent, suffering is certain; that which possesses suffering is not bliss. To this it is replied: This is true; however, as for what was said regarding its having causes—that was stated with reference to the relationship of cause and effect from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). As the venerable Ācārya [Nāgārjuna] has said: "Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand by any other language, so the world cannot be made to understand without recourse to worldly conventions."

And that bliss which has the characteristic of non-arising is designated as "beneficial for the present time" or "beneficial for the future time," because it is within the range of the Buddhas' vision, according to the principle that "reality is the range of the Buddhas' vision. Consequently, this remains established: just as in conventional reality there is the designation of the relationship between cause and effect.

(4) Having recited the three syllables, one should then draw the heart-mantra of Vajradhara with the ring finger using the sixth Conqueror [the letter *Ṣa*], and one should honor it with red flowers. (5)

Thereafter, one should worship with red flowers the *hṛdaya* (heart) of Vajradhara. "Vajra" refers to indivisible gnosis (*abhedyajñāna*); he who holds that is Vajradhara, the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*). His *hṛdaya* is called the *dharmodayā* because it cannot be revealed [externally]. It should be worshipped with red flowers such as *karavīra*. Having drawn [the design] with the ring finger of the left hand—that is, with the ring finger of the left hand—one should do so. By the "Sixth Victor," the Sixth Victor Vajrasattva is designated as the substance; this is because the effect is metaphorically applied to its cause, as it arises from that. Recited with the three syllables—namely, *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*—in the second sense, having drawn the lotus-heart of the perfectly awakened Vajradhara with the ring finger and moved it with the *vajra* (penis), so says the venerable Samvaranātha: "The knower of yoga should always lick [it] with the mouth of the ring finger and the thumb. By the "Sixth Victor," the Sixth is Vajrasattva; because he is the cause of its arising, the *bodhicitta* itself is called Vajrasattva through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause. By means of that which serves as the indicator, and not by means of the *prajñā*, the *bodhicitta* situated in the arising of the lotus should be employed, for then great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arises. Thus, in the *Ādibuddha*: "When the *bodhicitta*, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen, and when the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be accomplishment for one who is unconscious? Recited with the three syllables, meaning in the state of great bliss characterized by the non-dual unity of body, speech, and mind, one should worship with red flowers—that is, one should perform the worship with their pollen. 5

Thereafter, having placed the lotus-hand in the left [hand] over the vessel of the Primordial Supreme (Paramādya), one should perform the libation according to the instruction, starting from the touch of the shoulder. 6.

The connection [of the text] is: "thereafter, one should perform. *Vajra* refers to the cognition of perception; because it is the cause for the arising of that [cognition], the substance itself is designated by that term. By means of that, the *savana*—that is, the bath—is to be performed. Regarding *Suilha vajram athedyam*: *su* means "well" (*sukham*), and *icha* (in the variant *kha*) means "O second one, you who have destroyed life, O supreme primordial vessel," and so forth. *Vajrasavana* means having cast the lotus of the hand—the *karakamala*—into the *paramādya-pātra*. *Paramādya* means the *vajra*; its *pātra* is the vessel. Therein, according to the instruction—that is, without transgressing the instruction—one purifies the substance with the three-syllable mantra. Through the touch of the *śaya* (the hand), this is the intended meaning: by satisfying the host of deities residing in the hand, one places *hāṃ yoṃ* on the thumb (*tarjanī*), *hī moṃ* on the middle finger (*madhyamā*), *hoṃ hrī~* on the ring finger (*anāmikā*), *huṃ* on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), and *phaṭ 2* in the center of the hand. Having placed *oṃ va~* there and having satisfied them, one should contemplate the substance as one's own limbs and minor parts (*aṅga-pratyaṅga*) using the mantra of the Blessed Lady with the left hand. In the sense of the second [meaning], *paramādya-pātra* is so called because it is supreme (*parama*) due to its excellence, and because it is the primordial cause (*ādya*) of bliss (*sukha*). That very vessel is designated as the *vidyā-paṅkaja* (the lotus of wisdom), because it is the support of bliss. When that vessel has become the causal sign (*nimitta*), the lotus of the hand arises as bliss, and the *bodhicitta* arises as the *rātrī-tilaka* (the night-mark). That very lotus is so called because it is fully blossomed, desirable, and endowed with the highest qualities. Therefore, regarding *dakṣiṇettaraṃ*: since the element of passion (*rajas*) exists in the right, one casts the other—the element of the moon—into it, like the *avadhūti* wind, and having lifted it upward, one should perform the *vajra-savana*. When the *bodhicitta* reaches the *avadhūti*, it is then called *vajra*; by means of that, one should perform the *savana*, the bath. One should lead the *bodhicitta* into the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*) according to the instruction—that is, from the teacher’s instruction. Here, the feet of the Guru are to be taken as refuge. Through the touch of the *śaya* with the hand, one touches the *guru-vidyā* (the consort of the Guru); at that moment, the mind becomes possessed of passion (*sarāga*). And when the mind becomes possessed of passion, then the opening of the *avadhūti* occurs. When the *avadhūti* opens, at that very moment the *bodhicitta* pervades the wheel of great bliss. 6.

Having performed the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) and the *vṛddhāṅga-uṣṭhāṅga-ulisamāyoga* (the conjunction of the limbs, thumbs, and fingers), one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) using the mantra of the Supreme Sovereign Goddess. 7.

The connection [of the text] beginning with *pravidhāya* is "one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*. Having performed the *karanyāsa* according to the stated sequence by means of the mantras of the six deities, one should take the substance with the left hand using the thumb and ring finger, sprinkle it over the hands, and then perform the *aṅganyāsa* with the six *Vareśvarī* mantras. In this regard, one should place the mantra-syllables: *oṃ va~* at the navel, signifying the goddess Raktavarṇavārāhī; *hā~ yoṃ* at the heart, signifying the blue-colored goddess Yāminī; *hrī~ mo~* at the mouth, signifying the white-colored goddess Mohinī; *hrī~* at the head, signifying the yellow-colored goddess Sañcāriṇī; *hu~ hū~* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), signifying the green-colored goddess Saṃtrāsinī; and *phaṭ phaṭ* at the forehead, signifying the smoke-colored goddess Caṇḍikā. This is because there is no distinction between the mantra and the deity. Alternatively, those syllables should be meditated upon as the deities themselves through the transformation of each respective syllable. Then, Vajravārāhī is red in color, three-faced, and six-armed. Her root face is red, the left is blue, and the right is green. She holds a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* in her left hands, and a noose in her right. She holds a hook, a trident, and a severed head in her right hands. She stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. Yāminī is blue in color, single-faced, and four-armed. She holds a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a bell in her left hands, and a knife (*kartti*) in her right. Mohinī, Sañcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā are white, yellow, green, and smoke-colored respectively; they are all single-faced and four-armed. In the left hands of all of them are a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a bell; in the right hands are a *ḍamaru* and a knife. All of them stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, have loose hair, and possess three eyes. She who is white has the luster of the moon and bears the lunar disc; the others have the luster of the sun and bear the solar disc. This is the second meaning.

That which produces bliss (*sukha*) is the *kara* (the hand), namely the *bodhicitta*. Its "placement" (*nyāsa*) is its pervasion of all limbs through the union with the fingers of the elder [hand]. According to the statement: "The knower of yoga should always lick [it] from the mouth of the ring finger and the thumb through the union of the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the excellent *vajra*," and by the principle: "Having placed the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the *bodhicitta*; one should meditate on the entire form of the *dhātu*. One should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the six mantras of the Sovereign Goddesses. The form of the Purified Bhagavatī, consisting of the six deities to be described later, is to be visualized instantaneously immediately after emptiness. Following the meditation on emptiness, having performed the placement of the limbs and so forth for the forms of the goddesses of the sense bases, one should write the heart-mantra of Vajradhara and worship it with red flowers; this is how it should be understood.

Thereafter, one should slowly sprinkle [the image] with water produced from serpents, which is highly distinguished, contained in a cloth, and equal to the mantra born of the union of the red pigment upon the wheel-vajra, while reciting the Śrīvatsa-devī form-mantra for protection.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Thereafter, one should sprinkle the vessel without mantra," and so forth. The vessel is said to be "without mantra" (amantra). It is produced from the union of *raṅga* and *aruṇa*; *raṅga* is tin (*vaṅga*) and *aruṇa* is copper (*tāmra*). That which is born from their union—that is, their melting together—is "produced from the union of *raṅga* and *aruṇa*," meaning bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). It is "equal" because it is free from defects such as unevenness. Where should one sprinkle it? "Upon the Vajradhara. *Vajradhara* is so called because he holds (*dhārayati*) the *vajra* substance; "upon him" means upon the skull-cup (*kapāla*) containing *madana*.
The meaning is "having gone around."

"Bhujagabhavaiḥ" means produced from snakes; "bhujagaḥ" means a serpent or *nāga*. "Śaśakam" means for the sake of a rabbit. "Tatrabhavaiḥ" means originating therefrom; "sindūraiḥ" means with vermilion; "suviśiṣṭaiḥ" means excellent or superior; "sicayagataiḥ" means contained within a cloth—here "sicaya" meaning the interior of a garment. Herein is the instruction: one should scatter a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) with superior vermilion from a swinging-cloth device (*dolāpaṭayantra*) onto a menstruating woman's garment using the index finger (*tarjanī*). [The word] "slowly" (*śanakaiḥ*) is used.

The second meaning is as follows: he is the *Vajradhara* because he holds the *vajra*, which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Upon that lotus of wisdom (*prajñāpaṅkaja*) is the "red-juice" (*raṅgāru*) born of yoga; it is "equipped with mantra" (*samantra*), for *raṅga* means passion (*rāga*) and *aru* means the very peak of pride (*manya*), which is like the dawn-red (*aruṇa*). It is the filaments (*kiṃjalka*) of the lotus of knowledge (*vidyāpadma*). The "union" (*yoga*) is their meeting. That which is born from the union of the red juice and the dawn-red, accompanied by the great dawn-red, is the meaning of "ever-present bodhicitta. For this very reason, it is "equipped with mantra" because, through the departure of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there is the attainment of the omniscient gnosis (*sarvajñajñāna*). Therefore, it is strewn with the "vermilion dyes" (*sindūra-rāga*) produced from the serpent-born [elements].
With most excellent great dyes, as if applied to a silken cloth—that is to say, well-fastened—gradually and in succession.

Having carefully drawn a lotus with eight petals, one should write the Heart-mantra of the Jina there, and within its center, one should inscribe the row of mantras using a stylus made of bamboo.

Regarding the passage beginning with "there," the connection is that one should "draw the line of mantras.

Having drawn the wheel, the term *śikhikoṭika* means "having the tip of a crest"; that is to say, it refers to a triangle (*śikhikoṭika*), where the "crest" (*śikhin*) is fire (*vahni*) and its "tip" (*koṭi*) is its apex.

Regarding this instruction: a six-spoked wheel, which is the Heart of the Jina, must be drawn; its heart is also the heart [of the deity], because it is the cause for the arising of secret knowledge (*guhyajñāna*).
Within that—that is, in the center of that wheel—this mantra is not to be written with a stalk of *gāṅgeya* or a golden stylus in the left hand.
This is the second meaning.
The *jinahṛdayāhṛdayavidyā* is that very lotus, which is the wheel (*cakra*) because it is the abode of the wisdom of all the Victors (*jina*).

Having drawn the "peak of the peacock" (*śikhikoṭika*)—so called because it consists of the fiery splendor of the knowledge of the *koṭi*-yantra—one brings it into conjunction with the excellent vajra (*suvajra*). The meaning is that its "womb" (*garbha*) is the "well-formed womb" (*udgarbha*), which is the wheel of excellent emanation (*sunirmāṇacakra*).

One should write the *maṃtrālī*; it is called *maṃtra* because it protects the mind (*manaḥ-saṃtrāṇāt*), and its *ālī* is the row of *bodhicitta*. One should offer that stream of *bodhicitta* with a "gold pin" (*gāṅgeya-śalākā*). Because the *avadhūtī* is golden-red and because the *avadhūtī* is also possessed of passion (*sarāga*), it is therefore similar to a gold pin.

On the outer portion of the wheel, in the directions of the east, north, west, and south (arkidig), one should draw auspicious svastikas in sequence. Regarding the phrase "of the wheel" and so forth, the connection is: "one should draw auspicious svastikas."
The phrase "in a clockwise direction" refers to the outer part of the wheel;
it means in the directions of the east, north, west, and south, following the sequence of east, north, west, and south, moving counter-clockwise (vāmāvartta) with the left hand.
This is the second meaning.
On the outer portion of the wheel—that is, on the exterior of the *nirmāṇacakra*—in the directions of the east, north, west, and south (the direction of the Sun), or everywhere; this is the meaning.
One should draw svastikas.
A "beautiful svastika" refers to that wherein there is stability; one should apply this restriction everywhere.

Gradually and very slowly, by means of the left hand, the actions of holding the breath are performed; because of its similarity to that [process], the hand is positioned in front of the left nostril.

Having drawn forth the Vajradevī, caused her to enter, and bound her within the syllables of the mantra, one should satisfy her through the proper ritual procedure by reciting: *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

"Having drawn forth," and so forth.
The connection is that one should satisfy the Vajra Goddess.

Having drawn forth the Blessed Lady who dwells in the world of Kaniṣṭha, having caused her to enter one's own heart, and having bound her to the syllables of the mantra according to the ritual procedure.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:

having formed the *jvālāmudrā*, one should rotate it over the forehead in a counter-clockwise direction while gazing upward; then, preceded by the recitation of the syllable *pheṃ*, one should recite *jaḥ hūṃ vaḥ hoḥ*. Therein, with the syllable *jaḥ* comes summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), with *hūṃ* entry (*praveśana*), with *vaḥ* binding (*bandhana*), and with *hoḥ* pleasing (*toṣaṇa*).

The second meaning: having drawn forth Vajradevī, that is, Vajravārāhī in the form of Caṇḍālī, and having caused her to enter the avadhūtī, one binds her within the mantra-syllables. The mantra is bodhicitta; its syllables are emptiness. Having made her consist of that, one should satisfy her according to the ritual procedure. One should do this again and again, as is easy to understand according to the specific details.

Thereafter, one should perform various forms of worship for her, who is the embodiment of mantra, with foods to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked, possessing all desirable qualities.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadanu" and so forth:
the connection is that one should perform worship (*saparyām vidadhīta*), meaning one should offer adoration (*pūjām vidadhyāt*). This is the meaning.

The various and great [mantra] of that Vajradevī, who is in the form of a mantra, is written upon the surface of a mirror preceded by the application of vermilion; the remainder is easy to understand.
"With the qualities of desire," and so forth, means "with those that are more distinguished";
this is the second meaning.

One should perform worship (*saparyā*), that is, *pūjā*, once the *bodhicitta* has been awakened—this is what must be understood—as manifold [offerings] fashioned from the continuous stream of *bodhicitta*, consisting of the mantras whose nature is emptiness. "With edibles," and so forth, means "with forms (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]."
This very worship, accompanied by the great bliss of all desirable qualities, leads to the pacification of all conceptual constructions.

With various forces, accompanied by intoxication, and with the five most supreme offerings.
And with songs, instrumental music, dances, circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise.
