With various and numerous forces and troops, with offerings of meat and intoxicants mixed together, with the five grains—mung beans, black gram, lentils, barley, and wheat—and furthermore with the supreme and excellent [objects] of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch;
with songs, vajra-songs, the sounds of musical instruments and the like, with dances, and dances of foot-steps; and with circumambulations, prostrations, and praises—this is easy to understand.
The second meaning:

together with the *valas*, which are the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of the accumulation of flesh, the entry into the *anupalambha* (non-apprehension) must be performed; for this very reason, with the *bodhicitta* established in great bliss (*mahāsukha*) along with the *madana*, the remainder is as previously described.
Every day, every fortnight, or every month, on the tenth lunar day.
One who desires her accomplishment should perform the ritual of worship as it has been described.

The connection [of the verse] beginning with "every day" (*pratidivasam*) is that one should perform the ritual of worship as previously described. Whether daily, or every fortnight, or every month, or on the tenth lunar day (*tithi*), the person of even intellect—desiring the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of this Vajrayoginī and keeping in mind both mundane and supramundane accomplishments—should act thus; the intention is that this very Blessed Lady bestows the entire mass of all happiness.

Thus ends the first chapter, the Ritual for External Worship, in the commentary titled *Mahāmukhaprakāśikā*, composed by the monk Śrī Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), within the *Śrī-tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi*.
Then, having performed the ritual of external worship, the one of vast compassion [entered] the center of the sacrificial arena where the enemies had been destroyed.
One should meditate upon the previously described Goddess, whose heart is radiant with the splendor of the sun.
Now, the procedure for the meditation on Vajravārāhī is described.
The connection is as follows: "Then," and so forth, ending with "one should meditate on the Goddess.

One should cultivate that meditation previously described, which was taught by the Tathāgatas such as the Lord Dīpaṅkara and Śākyamuni; or alternatively, one should cultivate that meditation as previously stated, which was taught by Kāla.
"Possessing great compassion" means having vast compassion; "bodhicitta" means the perfectly complete body [of enlightenment].

"Nirmitārimadhyājo" means: upon the lotus in the center of the *nirmāṇacakra*, one should meditate on the Blessed Lady within the solar disc upon the heart of a lifeless corpse. "Vyasu" refers to one whose vital breaths (*asavaḥ*) have departed; his "heart" (*hṛdayam*) is the "heart of the lifeless" (*vyasuhṛdaya*). "Uṣṇagu" is that which has hot rays (*uṣṇāḥ gavaḥ*); its "disc" (*vimba*) is the "solar disc" (*uṣṇaguvimba*). Thus, "vyasuhṛdayoṣṇaguvimba" [means] the solar disc upon the heart of the lifeless. This is the meaning: one should meditate on the Blessed Lady upon the solar disc atop the heart of a deceased person on the lotus of the *nirmāṇacakra*.

This has been stated by the Blessed Lady: when the bodhicitta, having gone to the *maṇyagra* (the tip of the jewel) and returned, reaches the *nirmāṇacakra*, then whatever bliss arises is indicated by that corpse; its heart is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the solar disc is non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*), which illuminates like the sun because it destroys the darkness of all conceptual constructions.
In that regard, one should meditate on emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.
Of what kind?

The twilight has the color of vermilion; the seven horses of the sun have set with their mass of rays; may she, the destroyer of all afflictions, who bears in her left hand the shimmering moon of nectar, protect us.
She holds a very white lotus in her left hand, is adorned with a banner filled with blood, has her head encircled by the thunderbolt-like Kālī, and her hair is loosened with hands raised above. ||2||

"Saṃdhyā-sindūra" and so forth: she whose complexion is like that of twilight (saṃdhyā) and vermilion (sindūra); who possesses the splendor of the setting sun due to the rising of great passion (mahārāga)—the sun being "khara-kara-nikarāyasta," meaning its brilliance is destroyed by a mass of fierce rays; "khara" means intense, and "kara" means a ray; thus "khara-kara" is an intense ray, and "nikara" is a collection thereof—she by whom the splendor of the seven suns has been eclipsed by such a mass of fierce rays; the connection is that she is "bearing a knife" (kartivibhratīm).

She who destroys all suffering (*sarvārtihaṃtrī*), who strikes down all pain and affliction (*pīḍā*) by uprooting the defilements such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth; she who holds a flaying-knife (*kartī*) in her right hand—[this being] because the sun-element resides in the right [side], and because wisdom (*prajñā*) has a sharp nature, it is fitting that she holds the knife in the right hand—and who bears a lotus (*kamala*) in her left arm, which radiates the rays of infinite, shimmering nectar; [the connection is: "she who bears the lotus," thereby also demonstrating: "By me, through the joy of wisdom, the glorious *bodhicitta* of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*) is held. This is the construction.
The lotus symbolizes great bliss; it is exceedingly white because its nature is bodhicitta, and it is filled with red because its essence is great emptiness.

[She is] "rich in banners" (*dhvajāḍhyā*) because she is enriched by the banner; "greatly rich in the skull-staff" (*khaṭvāṅgana āḍhyo maha*) indicates the bearing of the *bodhicitta* in the *Avadhūtī*. [She is] "one whose head is surrounded by Dambholikālī"—here, *kālyā* refers to the row (*āliḥ*) of skulls (*mastaka*), and by that *kālī*, because of her bearing five skull-cups of emptiness (*śūnyapañcakapāla*), the bearing of *bodhicitta* is manifested in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). By "Dambholikālī," *dambholi* means a thunderbolt (*vajra*); *dambholika* is that which is a thunderbolt itself; *dambholikāli* is the row of those thunderbolts. By that *dambholikālī*, her head is "surrounded," meaning it is known in every respect. This indicates the bearing of enlightenment endowed with emptiness, because of her bearing a garland of thunderbolts on her forehead. "With hair loosened and hands in the sky" (*muktamūrddhā khe hastāṃ*): her hair is loosened, and her hands are raised up as they happen to be. Furthermore, of what kind? (Verse 2)

Her limbs are adorned with a garland of severed heads; blood flows from her mouth as she tastes it while uttering a loud roar. With a jackal-faced deity on her left hip, she possesses an excellent and auspicious gait, her face marked by the root of wrath.

Full of bliss and passion, endowed with various aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*), she dances in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). Her body is sealed with ritual gestures (*mudrās*), she is divested of clothing, sixteen years of age, and possesses a most beautiful form. || 3 ||
"Muṇḍālī," and so forth.

By holding the *āli* (vowels) and *kāli* (consonants), her body is adorned with a garland of severed heads (*muṇḍālī*). Blood flows from her mouth; she is red because she drinks the blood of emptiness from the four Māras at her shoulders and other parts, which is characterized by the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*)—the taste of the self-taste. She has six eyes (*ṣaṇṇetrā*), meaning her two faces each have three eyes. These represent the conventional and ultimate truths, as she perceives the three times in every aspect. She emits a continuous sound (*muktanādā*) due to being filled with the bliss of great ecstasy (*atyantānanda*).

On her left is a face with an upward-turned jackal (*kirā*) head, and on her right is a face with an upward-turned boar (*sūkara*) head; the boar face is held there because of the purification of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), since conventional reality has the nature of delusion (*moha*), and the boar is the very essence of delusion. She possesses excellent and auspicious gait, for she is the root of wrath yet her countenance is not fierce, as her nature is playful and graceful (*śṛṅgāra-lalita*). Her primary face is full of bliss (*sānandā*) because she constantly maintains the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); she is full of passion (*sānurāgā*) because of the uninterrupted arising of great passion (*mahārāga*). She is endowed with various flavors (*rasa*) due to the union with the nine channels (*nāḍī-rasa*). She performs the dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) because she proceeds to the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*). Her limbs are sealed by the six mudrās; she is called a "mudrā" because she bestows joy (*muda*) and delight (*harṣa*), and her body is marked by those possessing the mudrās—namely, the six ornaments such as the wheel, earrings, necklace, bracelets, girdle, and thread—due to the purification of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). She is without clothing because of the abandonment of the veil of ignorance regarding what is to be known (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). She is sixteen years old due to the purification of the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*). She is of exquisite form because her body is produced from the accumulation of merit gathered over hundreds of thousands of eons. || 3 ||
Having performed the ritual for the summoning of wisdom and other rites for the Blessed Lady as previously described, the mantra-knower, skilled in the procedures, [should proceed].
One should meditate upon a single wheel, revolving toward the face of a swastika and a lotus. || 4 ||
"Jñānākarṣa," and so forth.
The connection is that one should meditate on the svastika.

Having performed the summoning of the wheel of command (ājñācakra) according to the stated sequence, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī), who is a knower of the ritual (vidhānavit)—that is, one who knows the procedure as it is prescribed—[should proceed].
Facing the *alika* (the forehead), moving rapidly and swiftly like a potter's wheel near the face of a bee, [it revolves] once or twice. || 4 ||
Thereafter, in the element of space, within a cave of Mount Trikūṭa, one should meditate upon the previously described blazing red wheel as it revolves. || 5 ||
"Following that," and so forth.
The connection is "from the meditation on the wheel.

Just as previously stated in the *Sindūra-pūjā*, it is filled with the syllables of the mantra as indicated by the wheel; likewise, in the element of space (*viyat-dhātu*), that is, in the element conjoined with the sky, [one meditates on] the *dharmodayā*.
Within the cave of the three-peaked mountain (*trikūṭa-giri*), in the center of a three-petalled lotus, it dwells rotating like the wheel of a potter, because of its excellence.
There, blazing with extreme velocity like a lamp in a windless place that remains steady and unshaken,
he caused the vast circle of faces— which was performing a libation with the essence of nectar dripping from them— to melt away.
Regarding that, the phrase "as if steady" and so forth is to be connected with the previously mentioned instruction, "one should meditate upon that wheel.
"As if steady" means because of extreme velocity—it is exceedingly so—just like a lamp burning in a windless place without flickering; this is easily understood. One should cause it to melt.

The wheel of the wide mouth has its essence made from the nectar of fame; this seat established by the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is the wheel situated between the anus and the genitals, which should be meditated upon. Herein, a brief instruction is stated.

First of all, one should diligently make the mind possessed of passion through the application of the three lotuses of knowledge. By means of the sequence of the *sagadhāga* [the downward-moving wind], from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) it goes to the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*); from the wheel of enjoyment to the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*); from the wheel of dharma to the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*); from the wheel of emanation to the wheel at the base of the vajra; from the wheel at the base of the vajra to the center of the vajra; and from the center of the vajra to the tip of the vajra. There, the glorious bodhicitta arises as a bliss characterized by non-arising (*anutpāda*). Abiding in that very bliss, one should once again cause that bodhicitta to turn back and enter the *avadhūtī*.
One should contemplate and meditate upon [the deity] as being dissolved in vapor upon the surface of a stainless mirror.

In this regard, the array of the dust-particles of the venerable Vajraguru is to be cultivated, while the bodhicitta—the forest of all goals—is not to be abandoned; for through its abandonment, detachment would arise. Thus, it was spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One in the *Sekoddeśa*:
"Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the passion of emission, by which the yogi comes face-to-face with liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra."
Even one who is lustful does not seek the science of erotics once he has become dispassionate.
I have said: furthermore, what suffering does the yogi seek therein?
He should accomplish the supreme syllable by means of the nature of the white syllable.
When the substratum has undergone transformation, there is detachment from that which is supported.
The relationship between the support and the supported continues as long as the state of the imperishable (akṣaratā) persists.
The mind has attained the state of the unchanging; it does not possess the characteristics of support and supported.
And therefore, without maintaining the bodhicitta, enlightenment is not attained; as it is said in the Śrī Kālacakra:
In the center, there is the entry of the vital breath; in the right and left channels, there is the binding of the movement of the moon in the lake.
When the mind is engaged with the mudrā, there is the attainment of supreme bliss and the vajra-binding.

Today, the sound of the Vajra, which is like a mass of easily obtainable water for the sake of happiness, is the milk born from the seed; it brings bliss and removes the fear of death—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru.
Therefore, O best of seekers, exert yourself toward perfect enlightenment. || 5 ||
One should perceive the three bodies as having the nature of the supreme innate state, pervading the world, radiating an immeasurable continuum of light; thereafter [one experiences] bliss. 6.
Now, he describes the beautiful form of the wheel belonging to that one endowed with great bliss.
"Regarding 'the three bodies,' and so forth..."

Therein, within the *dharmakāya*, is the form of the *dharmasambhoga* and *nirmāṇa*. The *dharmakāya* transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is to be known by the omniscient one, its nature is emptiness, and its characteristic is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The *sambhogakāya* is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; it is produced from the accumulation of merit, characterized by the cessation of the activity of mind and mental factors, and is accessible only to Bodhisattvas. The *nirmāṇakāya* is born from the power of former vows and the ripening of skillful means for those to be trained; like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), it is free from conceptual construction and fulfills all intentions. Because this intrinsic nature is the supreme immortality, and because these three bodies share a single essence whose innate nature is co-emergent (*sahaja*), it is called the *mahāsukhakāya*. This very [body] has the characteristic of union (*yuganaddha*), being the single flavor of the conventional and the ultimate. How is the unity of the conventional and the ultimate understood? Since the conventional consists of the nature of phenomena (*bhāvasvabhāva*) and the ultimate consists of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatāsvarūpa*), how can there be unity between two things that are mutually contradictory? To this, the following response is given: the Tathāgata, from his own perspective, is one whose mind has ceased.

Being mental (*caitta*), it is indeed of the beautiful form of emptiness; thus, because it arises as a manifestation for the sake of those to be trained (*vineya*) until their minds are exhausted, there is no contradiction. Like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), it is rightly said to fulfill the intentions of all people. However, [one might object]: "If this body remains while the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) have ceased, then since the body is dependent upon both body and mind, that fault follows. To this we reply: It remains throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) because it is produced from the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*); thus, by the power of the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*), it persists.

Furthermore, there would be the cessation of mind and mental factors; therefore, everything remains in its own natural state. For this very reason, it pervades the entire world, because every phenomenon possesses a nature of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*). Since its continuum is a radiance of immeasurable peace due to its indestructible nature, it is "radiant infinite bliss"—this is the meaning. "One should see" means one should discern it.

Because it is possible to perceive [the mind] right there when it is directed toward the present and possesses subsequent happiness, he explains the application to the cultivation of subsequent happiness. || 6 ||
One should contemplate this every day, at every twilight, or whenever there is an opportunity.
This is clearly stated as long as the signs of accomplishment have not yet appeared. || 7 ||
The connection is with the phrase "every day" and so forth, ending with "one should contemplate";
that is, this aforementioned great bliss (mahāsukha) should be contemplated every day or at each junction of the day (pratisandhya).

Whenever the wind enters the *avadhūtī*—meaning at the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), or at every moment, or indeed always—as long as the sign of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*), that is, the cause (*nimitta*) of the accomplishment (*siddhi*) which is Mahāmudrā, has not arisen, one should clearly meditate upon this in all circumstances. First, this sign of accomplishment is stated as follows, which will be explained hereafter. Thus he says: || 7 ||
When this [state] becomes clearly manifested through the continuous connection with joy and absorption that arise without effort;
If there is no pain from lashes, slaps, and the like here, then success will be near at hand. || 8 ||
"Born of effortlessness" means that through constant practice, because joy follows without exertion, due to its stability,
this [object] becomes clearly manifested, that is, it becomes more distinct.

Regarding this, it is said: "There is no pain from whips, slaps, and so forth; a whip is a leather strap, and a slap is a blow with the hand. If, when one strikes oneself with such things, no pain occurs, then it should be understood that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is not far off—that is, accomplishment has become imminent. (8)
He states another sign as well.
If the sharp sound of beaten drums and other instruments does not fall within the range of hearing;
When unsurpassed enlightenment is attained here, even in a dream, it is the supreme accomplishment of one who has long practiced meditation.

If the sound of beaten instruments— such as the *paṇava* (small drum), *mardala* (kettledrum), and by the word "etcetera," the *ḍhakkā*, *bherī*, and so forth— which have been struck intensely, greatly, and in a grand manner, does not become a great noise that exceeds the range of perception or becomes an object of auditory consciousness,
he states another sign:

When unsurpassed awakening is attained even in a dream—if a yogi perceives himself as a perfectly enlightened Buddha (samyaksambuddha) in a dream—then the supreme accomplishment of one who possesses meditative concentration will soon be realized; thus, for a yogi engaged in the cultivation of great bliss, the foremost accomplishment, the state of Vajradhara, will certainly come to pass. || 6 ||
Having observed this cause for success, he states what ought to be done:
For the sake of accomplishing thirst [for dharma], one should resort to the path of the ancestors, such as at the roots of trees and so forth.
Dwelling there, the wise one should constantly practice the yoga of the generation stage. || 10 ||

"Having seen," and so forth: the wise one should perform the yoga of the generation stage (*utpannakrama*); the meaning is that he should cultivate great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Constantly" means without interruption. In a cemetery, at the foot of a mountain, in a grove, at the root of a tree, and so forth—"cemetery" (*pitṛvana*) means a charnel ground; "mountain" (*giri*) means a peak; "grove" (*kuñja*) means a bower of creepers; "root of a tree" is easy to understand; and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), empty houses and the like are included. Dwelling—that is, staying—in such a place, the yogi will very quickly realize the meditative absorption of great bliss (*mahāsukha-samādhi*) due to the absence of mental distraction.
Regarding what occurs when meditative concentration (samādhi) is accomplished, he says: ||10||

Since the dissolution of the earth and the other elements occurs in an ascending order, that which is then known is the reality: luminosity, resembling the sky, and consisting of pure gnosis alone. (1)
Regarding the phrase "in the case of accomplishment" (*siddhau*) and so forth:

for the earth and the other elements, there occurs a process of successive dissolution (*laya*). Specifically, the dissolution of earth, water, fire, air, consciousness, and the rest is described as follows: therein, the element of earth is dissolved into water; water into fire; fire into air; air into the mind (*citta*); the mind into the mental objects (*caitya*); the mental objects into ignorance (*avidyā*); knowledge (*vidyā*) into the Radiant One (*prabhāsvara*). Thus it has been said:
“The earth element dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into the subtle element; and the wind dissolves into consciousness.”

The mind dissolves into mental factors, and mental factors dissolve into ignorance; that [ignorance] too goes into the luminous (*prabhāsvara*). This is cessation within the three realms. If this is so, what would occur? Then, "appearance" (*khyāti*) shines forth. Cessation is like the sky, resembling space because of the departure of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); it is the luminous, stainless, mere cognition (*jñāna-mātra*), comparable to an illusion. Therefore, it is said here to be truly supreme. [Objection: When everything has ceased, how can even cognition remain, since it is dependent upon an object of knowledge (*jñeya*)?
It should not be said that mere cognition, which has emptiness as its characteristic, is by nature empty, like an illusion, and devoid of conceptual construction; for that is not negated here.
Thus it was said by the glorious Lord Śākya:

Just as the blackness in water is destroyed by contact with a wound [or medicinal application], so too that impurity which exists within the sattva is not destroyed; rather, it remains because of its stainless nature.

In the same way, the impurity of the mind is destroyed through union with emptiness, but its nature as knowledge is not destroyed; it remains established in its stainlessness. Just so, the impurity of the mind is destroyed by that very union with emptiness, but its nature as knowledge is not destroyed; it remains established in its stainlessness.

Consequently, although the nature of things is empty and only consciousness exists, at the very first moment of the arising of that cognition, signs arise for the purpose of focused application. || 11 ||
One should recognize it by its signs; indeed, those who know it understand that signs are fivefold.
Therefore, a yogi who is concentrated should perceive those [objects] with the mind.

"One should know," and so forth. This refers to the mindless knowledge (*niścitta-jñāna*) by means of its signs (*nimitta*). As for how many those various signs are, they are known to be of five kinds; those who know them are "knowers" (*tajjña*), meaning those who are expert in their meaning. For that very reason, the yogi, joined with *samādhi*, should observe those signs with the mind, as the signs arise in succession. || 13 ||
Regarding that, he states the sequence:
first is the appearance of a mirage; the second sign is the form of smoke.
The third is like a firefly, and the fourth is clearly radiant like a lamp. || 13 ||
"First," and so forth:

resembling a mirage, like a shimmering heat-haze, the second sign has the form of smoke; this third is clearly like a firefly; and the fourth is a blazing light, like the flame of a lamp, distinct and manifest. || 13 ||
He states the fifth sign:
The fifth sign is luminous and free from conceptual construction, resembling a cloudless sky.
Thus, having obtained the sign, one attains the great mudrā. || 14 ||
It is like a cloudless sky, radiant like the stainless firmament, and free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), because at that moment the mind and mental factors are stilled.

Having thus obtained the sign (*nimitta*)—meaning the yogi has attained the sign through the aforementioned sequence—he obtains the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is indeed the Great Gesture (*mudrā*). The meaning is that he shall directly realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*) endowed with all supreme aspects. (14)
Desiring to rise, having prostrated to the Yoginī and the Lord, and having uttered "mūḥ" and "kṛti," he remains standing.
Having arisen, one whose intellect is fixed on reality should perform his duty; the knower of yoga should always remain joined in the practice of yoga. 15.
Thus ends the procedure for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the perfect attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 2 ||
"Desiring to arise," and so forth:

when one wishes to arise from that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then, having prostrated to and paid homage to the Yoginī Vajravārāhī, and having invoked the Lord situated upon the head by uttering the *mūriti* mantra, one should rise and perform one's duties. One whose intellect possesses the wisdom of the three natures of reality should then remain in the state of the Great Bliss of Yoga, which is the gnosis of the meditative absorption of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*) through the ego-sense of the union. || 15 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, the Procedure for Meditative Cultivation, in the *Mahāsukhaprakāśikā* (The Illumination of Great Bliss), composed by the monk Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Madhyamaka, for the sake of perfecting the knowledge of reality.
And he was attended by many disciples who had formed circles, with their hands joined in salutation at his lotus-like feet.
On the tenth lunar day, the minister should bestow grace upon them.
Now, for the purpose of initiating disciples, it is said:
"Being requested," and so forth.

"Requested" means entreated many times, in various ways, by disciples who have formed a *maṇḍala*—those by whom a *maṇḍala* has been made, preceded by the performance of the *maṇḍala*, the Guru should be requested with their feet like lotuses bowed down (*padābjanataiḥ*), that is, by those whose speech is accompanied by mantras (*vimaṃtraiḥ*). On the tenth lunar day (*daśamī-tithau*) and no other day, the Knower of Mantras (*mantra-jñaḥ*) should perform, that is, bestow, grace and compassion (*anugraha-kṛpām*) upon those disciples. || 1 ||

Having fully worshipped the Goddess who is the embodiment of mantra, and having taken up that primordial Goddess who resides within the wheel (cakra) while reciting the mantra, one who has performed the prescribed yoga should emerge from that [state]. || 2 ||

"Having worshipped her in the form of the mantra," and so forth. Having worshipped the Goddess who is the very nature of the mantra—as described in the section on the worship with vermilion—he says that very thing: "She who resides in the wheel," meaning she who resides in the six-spoked wheel; "one who has performed yoga," meaning one who has achieved meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), or else one whose form is non-different from the Blessed Lady; "having taken," meaning having grasped [the substance], he should purify it by reciting the mantra of the Blessed Lady.

"Go forth from that place of worship of the Bhagavatī, the Supreme Primordial One. This means that within the tantra, the Bhagavatī is worshipped; one should offer a cloth painting (*paṭa*) and so forth. Then, having worshipped the Bhagavatī, one should take from that location substances purified by mantra and go outside.
The intention is: "for the sake of the disciple. || 2 ||
Then the Guru should look upon the disciple standing at his right side, who has performed the fivefold circumambulation, who wears a garland of flowers, and who has meditated upon the Lord.
"Then," and so forth;
the connection is that "he should look at the disciple.
This means [the disciple] has performed prostration with his two knees, two hands, and head, having completed the five-pointed salutation (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*).

With his teeth emerged, having renounced all his possessions, wearing a garland of flowers and holding a sacred wreath with both hands—he who has meditated upon that Lord as his Guru on his head; "Guru" here means "the Teacher. || 3 ||
And thereafter, as previously described, the wheel of goddesses radiates forth rays with great speed.
Having meditated upon him as being within his own body, the wielder of the vajra should bestow it upon him. || 3 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with *tadanu* and so forth:

immediately thereafter, having meditated upon—having contemplated—the aforementioned wheel of the Goddess (*devīcakra*), which possesses six spokes, is complete with the syllables of the mantra, has emerging rays, is shimmering with radiance, and is whirling with speed; having thus visualized such a wheel, one should then place it upon the body of the resident disciple—that is, upon his body at the *nirmāṇacakra*. What should be done after that? One should bestow the "vajra-holder" [the vessel] upon him; then, one should hand over the full vessel to the disciple, and everything therein must be consumed by the disciple.
Therefore, it is the instruction that [it] is Madana. || 3 ||
Thus there may be possession, its bud-like tremor, or tears.
In the morning, the arising of knowledge and one's own true nature are to be perfected. || 4 ||
"Thus," and so forth.

In this sequence, possession (*āveśa*) occurs; therein, possession is of various kinds: possession of body (*kāyāveśa*), possession of speech (*vāgāveśa*), and possession of mind (*cittāveśa*). Among these, in possession of body, there arise ripples [of emotion], horripilation, and trembling of the limbs; there is the shedding of tears of joy, and one falls to the ground. In possession of mind, the arising of knowledge and the manifestation of one's own true nature occur spontaneously. In possession of speech, there is unprecedented discourse, which is consistent and conveys the knowledge of the Omniscient One; he speaks exhaustively and in due order. Alternatively, if possession does not occur for one of meager merit, then this following procedure should be performed.

One should consecrate the five limbs of a goat with the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas; one should prepare equal portions of great oil and great guggulu. By means of that, when the mantra is recited, entry [into the deity] certainly occurs through the mere inhalation of its breath. || 5 ||
Thereafter, one should explain the meditative absorption (samādhi) and the mantra for the worship of Vajrayoginī.
For one endowed with faith and virtue, who is a true devotee inseparable from the Guru and the Buddha. || 6 ||
Regarding the phrase "tadanu" and so forth:
one should explain the "samādhi of samādhi," which means the samādhi of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

With the worship mantra of Vajrayoginī, for one who is endowed with faith, virtuous, and wise, and who possesses true devotion toward the Guru as inseparable from the Buddha—since there is no difference between those two—the Guru is viewed just as one views the Teacher. || 6 ||
One should not explain this yoga to those whose minds are immediately devoid of faith, even though it is easily perfected and provides immediate conviction.
Of a disciple devoid of devotion. || 7 ||
"By not speaking," and so forth.

One should neither speak nor reveal this aforementioned yoga, which produces immediate realization through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which generates conviction in a friend, and which bestows excellent accomplishment—the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) that grants perfect attainment—to a disciple who is devoid of faith, whose mind has abandoned faith, and who lacks devotion. (7)
Now, moreover, he speaks of the benefits of seeing [the Buddha].
For one who is joined with the mantra.
But for him who performs worship of the circle of goddesses, the eight fears and the great sins depart.
"Vidadhati," and so forth.

For one who performs the mantra-worship of the Goddess’s wheel—the six-spoked wheel of the Blessed Vajravārāhī, which is joined with mantras and perfected by mantras—her eight fears depart; the fears of lions, elephants, fire, serpents, thieves, fetters, and water depart and flee away. Great sins, even the five actions of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karmāṇi*), also flee away. || 8 ||
Misfortune, poverty, disease, old age, suffering, and dejection; delusion, strife, impurity, and afflictions, as well as various kinds of pain. || 6 ||

"Unfortunate," and so forth. In this world, one becomes endowed with supreme good fortune; [the following] depart: poverty (dāridrya), which is lack of wealth; disease (vyādhi), which is bodily affliction; old age (jarā), which is decrepitude; verbal sensation (vācikī vedanā); mental sensation (caitasikī vedanā), which is dejection (daurmanasya); delusion (bhrama), which is error (bhrānti); strife (kali), which is dispute (vivāda); impurity (kaluṣa), which is sin (pāpa); the afflictions (kleśa), namely passion, hatred, and delusion (rāga-dveṣa-moha); and the calamities of planetary influences (graha) and the like. The connection is that these various (nānāvidhā)—meaning of many kinds (aneka-prakārā)—depart. || 6 ||

"He who recites the wheel-mantra, having meditated upon it in the heart with speech restrained—he, having attained perfection, obtains the eight [siddhis] as well as the five superknowledges and the eight qualities.
Regarding the phrase "he who recites," and so forth:

Having meditated upon and contemplated the mantra of the wheel together with the wheel within his heart by means of mental restraint and speech, that practitioner of mantra attains the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*): the power of ointment, the power of the pill, the power of the sandals, the power of medicinal herbs, the power of jewels, the power of mantras, the power of yakṣa-women, and the power of entering another's body. Furthermore, he attains the five superknowledges (*abhijñās*): the divine ear, the divine eye, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former existences, and the knowledge of miraculous powers; as well as the eight qualities (*guṇas*): minuteness (*aṇimā*), lightness (*laghimā*), greatness (*gaṇimā*), attainment (*iṣitva*), sovereignty (*vaśitva*), mastery (*kartṛtva*), subjugation (*bhojyatva*), and the fulfillment of every wish (*icchāprakāmajā*). These are the eight qualities. || 10 ||

He who meditates with effort upon her whose face is like the sun at the four junctions of the day every single day—she whose form cannot be conquered by Hari, Hara, or Hiraṇyagarbha—that person conquers. 11.
"Contemplating," and so forth:

That practitioner who daily contemplates with effort the boar-faced Kolāsyā during the four junctions of the day—at dawn, midday, sunset, and midnight—he conquers death in its embodied form, which cannot be conquered even by Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha. (11)

For him who meditates upon Aśanikolamukhī together with her wheel, there arise vast lands abounding in clothing, food, drink, wealth, and grain; celestial palaces, divine beds, seats, and requisites; and various beloved sciences. (12)
Thus concludes the procedure for favoring disciples, together with its benefits, for the sake of the perfect attainment of the knowledge of reality.

"From clothing, food," and so forth: clothing (*vastra*) means garments; food (*anna*) refers to edible items; drink (*pāna*) refers to milk and the like; wealth (*dhana*) refers to gold and the like; grain (*dhānya*) refers to rice and so on; vast land (*viśālabhūmi*) means a great expanse of earth; a palace (*prāsāda*) means a celestial bed (*divyaśayana*) and the like; a seat (*āsana*) means a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) and the like; and "means" (*sādhanāni*) refers to platforms (*mañca*). All these things belong to that minister.

He who meditates upon her whose face is like a boar, who has the face of a boar, who possesses a wheel, and who is endowed with two half-wheels—[surrounded] by celestial women, various sciences, and diverse arts and crafts—[attains success]. Thus ends the third chapter, "The Procedure for Benefiting Disciples along with its Benefits," in the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi-ṭīkā* composed by the monk Madhyamakaruci.
Now, therefore, the extraction of the mantra, which has come down through the lineage of gurus, is written as the secret of the mantra.
I shall now set forth the supreme extraction of the mantra, which has come from ear to ear and from mouth to mouth—the heart of Vajrayoginī—according to its sequence. (1)
"Regarding the words 'maṃtra' and so forth:

hereafter, following what was previously stated, I shall describe the extraction of the mantra—the heart-essence of Vajrayoginī and the heart-essence of Kolamukhī—which has been transmitted from ear to ear, having come down through a lineage of oral tradition due to its extreme sacredness. (1)
Having drawn a wheel as previously described, provided with the abodes of the hosts of Maruts.
There, one who has completed the sequence should likewise draw the vowels (ālikāli) and the corners.
"Beginning with 'pūrvodita' and so forth: one should draw the wheel in the form of the *dharmodayā* as if it were previously described.

Endowed with the abode of the hosts of Maruts—that is, possessing forty-nine squares—one should write the *ālikāli* (vowels and consonants) there in the wheel according to the sequence, that is, in due order."
Starting from the letter *a* up to the sixteen vowels, and from the letter *ka* up to the letter *ha*;
for this very reason, the triangular arrangement is called the sequence of expansion (*prastāva*).
One, three, five, seven, and especially nine; eleven, and the tenth characterized by the addition of three—this is the definition of the grid (*koṣṭha*).
One should write them there in sequence, one above the other.

Having rendered the vowels (āli) and consonants (kāli) empty by means of the syllable *kṣa*, the wise one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). The door is established as the imperishable (*akṣara*) together with the *prati*. (2)
Joined with that which resides below *ja*, situated below *ḍa*, and adorned below *ha*.
Having first written the three syllables, that six-syllable mantra illuminates the reality.

"Bhārageyādi" and so forth. The connection with "everywhere" is as follows: one should write the vowel *a*, which is situated below the letter *ka* (the "lower-positioned" of *ka*), as "bhādharaga. One should write the vowel *u*, which is situated below the letter *i* (the "lower-positioned" of *i*), as "ḍādharastha," adorned by that which is below the letter *ha* (the "lower-positioned" of *ha*). This refers to the letter *ma*, which is below *ha*; it is "adorned" (*vibhūṣita*) by that "lower-positioned" of *ḍa*. When there is a conjunction of the vowels *a* and *u*, the result is *o*; that *o* is adorned by the letter *ma*. The meaning is the syllable *oṃ*. One should first write this triad.
... illuminating the reality of the six syllables, it reveals the supreme reality of the syllables. || 3 ||
The *bhoddha* should be placed at the beginning, followed by the *choddha*; then the *sthitasametaṭoddhu* should be written, and after that, the *sthita*.
Joined with the lower *ḍa*, it is the support of *ṣa*; joined with the upper *ṣa*, it has gone to the upper state. || 4 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *bhoga*: the letter *va* situated above the letter *bha*; the letter *va* situated above the letter *cha*; joined with the letter *ṭa* situated above [the previous]; the letter *ra* should be written below it; joined with the lower part of *ḍa*, meaning the letter *ḍha* which is the lower part of *ḍa*; joined with the letter *va* situated below *ṣa*; joined with the letter *dha* situated above *ṣa*; joined with the letter *du* situated above the letter *śa*. || 4 ||
That which is situated below the lower lip joined with *u* is established above the upper lip joined with *ṭa*.
Thereafter, one should visualize the syllable *gaṃ*, conjoined with the letter *ṭha* and the vowel *a*, situated within the heart and accompanied by the mantra *aiṃ vāma*. || 5 ||
"Below," and so forth: the letter *ḍa*, which is situated below the letter *la* and joined with the vowel *ā* (the lower part of *na*);

then the letter *ka*, which is situated above the letter *pa* and joined with the vowel *i* (the lower part of *ṭa*); and the letter *na*, which is situated above the letter *pha* and accompanied by the vowel *ī* (the lower part of *ṭha*).

The letter *ai* (the left side of *aikāra*) situated between *ha* and *ṭa*, together with the letter *e* (the left side of *aikāra*), and the letter *ya* situated between *ha* and *ṭa* (between *ha* and *ṭaṃ*). || 5 ||

Following that, [place] *ca* situated between *sa* and *ma*, joined with *ṭha* on its right; then *bha* well-positioned below it; then *tha* situated between *ha* and *tha*, joined with *ta* on its left; and finally *pa* situated between *ṭha* and *la*.

One should draw the letter *va* situated between *ca* and *ka*; then the letter *bha*, well-positioned below and joined with the *ṭha* on its left; then the letter *ja*, well-positioned below the *tha* and joined with the *ṛ* (repha) to its right; then the letter *va* situated between *ha* and *tha*; then the letter *ṇa* to the left of the *ta* and joined with that [va]; then the letter *ra* situated between *la* and *ṭha*. 6.

[The seed-syllable] situated in the middle of *sarvakarāntaka* (the end of all hands), joined with the first letter of the third group (*ga*) from the left, conjoined with the upper part of *ṇa*, standing above *la*, situated below *cha*, and joined with the right side of *ṭha*. || 7 ||

The letter *pha* is at the end of all [the consonants]; the first of the third group (*ta*) is joined with the leftward vowel (*ī*). The letter *aḥ* is taken from all the vowels; the letter *pha* and the letter *na* are between them. The first of the third group is *ṭa*; it is joined with the leftward vowel (*ī*), thus becoming *ṭī*. It is conjoined with *ṇa*. The lower part of *la* is the vowel *u* of the letter *śa*; it is joined with that, thus becoming *lū*. It is situated below the lower part of *la*. The upper part of *cha* is the letter *va* situated above the letter *cha*; it is situated at the base of *bha*, joined with the rightward *ṭha*, thus becoming *bhṛ*. It is conjoined with that. 7.
The letter *tha* joined with *ga*, and below it the letter *tha* joined with *ga*, followed by the letter *ṇa* below [the previous].
The letter *pha* is joined with the lower lip (*ṭa*), the letter *tha* is joined with the upper lip (*ga*), and the letter *la* is joined with the lower lip (*ḍha*). || 8 ||

The letter *takāra* with the vowel *aikāra* situated above it; joined with that, the letter *bakāra* below the letter *ṭhakāra*; then the letter *ṇakāra* below the letter *thakāra* conjoined with the vowel *okāra* situated above it; then the letter *cakāra* below the letter *phakāra*; joined with the letter below *ṭhakāra*, the letter *nakāra* situated above the letter *phakāra*.
That which is joined with the upper part of the letter *ṇa*, namely the letter *e*, and joined with that, together with the letter *ya* situated below the letter *la*. || 8 ||
And the jewel-studded ground stands elevated, consisting of three tiers.
Accompanied by the lower *ḍā* and the void (*śūnya*), joined with the lower *thā*, situated in the lower *śā*, and also conjoined with the lower *jā*. || 6 ||

The letter *ḍa* joined with the lower part [of *tha*] (the vowel *a*) and the void (*śūnya*, the nasal *anusvāra*), together with the letter *va* which is below *ta* and joined with the void (*anusvāra*), and the letter *ha* situated above; the letter *pha* is joined with *ra* and *ta* and *la*; by this, the triad *phat* is to be understood. Joined with the lower part of *tha* (the vowel *a*), joined with the lower part of *śa* (the vowel *a*), and also joined with the lower part of *bha* (the vowel *a*), as well as the letter *ca* which is the lower part of *tha*, and joined with the lower part of *śa* (the vowel *a*), and also joined with the lower part of *ba* (the vowel *a*), and joined with the lower part of *a* (the vowel *ā*)—that is to say, joined with the vowel *ā*. || 6 ||
This secret mantra of the goddess Aśanī, composed of the syllables *jha-bā-ma-ga* situated in the center of *sa-ya*, should be written, recited, and meditated upon.

The meaning is that one should take the letter *ha*, which is situated between *sa* and *ka*—that is, between the letters *sa* and *ka* accompanied by *jha*—and join it with the vowel *a* located to the left of the letter *ka*.

This is the secret [mantra] formed from the aforementioned syllables. Having extracted this secret from the first syllable beginning with *ka* among the stated letters, it is called "secret" because it is the cause of that [attainment]. What is this secret? It means this is the mantra of the goddess Aśanī, Vajravārāhī. What should be done with this mantra? To this he says: "It should be written, recited, and meditated upon"—meaning it must be inscribed, chanted, and visualized.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial tree, the excellent jar, and even the glorious cow of plenty—these, when propitiated, bestow wealth here; but he alone grants happiness along with prosperity.
Thus, in the accomplishment of the knowledge of reality, the procedure for extracting the mantra is as follows:

the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), the jewel, the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the foremost pitcher (*agrakumbha*), the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), the glorious wish-cow (*śrīkāmadhuk*), and the cow of plenty (*śrīkāmadhenu*)— whatever else is praised and renowned, when these are practiced, they bestow wealth.
Furthermore, in this world, this King of Mantras bestows supramundane bliss—that is, great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—along with wealth;

the meaning is that it is accompanied by riches. Other [mantras], when accomplished, yield only wealth and not unsurpassed bliss. This one, however, grants everything. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims in every way at all times, and as the cause for mundane and supramundane attainments, this alone should be practiced by those seeking enlightenment.

Thus ends the procedure for the extraction of mantras in the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi-ṭīkā* composed by the monk Śrī Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Middle Way (*madhyamaka-ruci*). Once this has been inscribed upon a vessel, the knower of the ritual should perform the protection of a child according to the rules for the sake of worship; it should be bound upon the arm, the neck, the crest-lock, or the head.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yasmin" and so forth:

having written this King of Mantras on a vessel such as a mirror according to the prescribed rite for the purpose of worship, a knower of the ritual should duly perform the protection of the child—that is, the protection of the infant—preceded by the worship of the Blessed Lady. Bound with that [thread] together with the mantra using vermilion (sindūra), where? On the arms, the neck, the crest-lock, and the two beautiful hands.
At the throat and at the crest-lock.
Upon seeing him, serpents flee along with their young, as do spirits, planetary deities, night-stalkers, and hosts of piśācas.
Other terrifying beings who cause fear to children likewise run away, distressed by fear of his strength, just as forest-dwelling lions flee from a powerful man.

"Having seen," and so forth: serpents, including snakes, flee; and *bhūtas*, *grahas*, night-stalkers (*niśicara*), and even hosts of *piśācas* flee from the child who is accompanied by protection (*sarakṣam*). Others as well—*ḍākinīs* and the like—who cause fear to children, being most terrible and supremely fearsome, [flee].
Here, he provides an illustration:

Just as forest-dwelling animals and the like flee upon seeing a lion—what kind of lion? One who is powerful and strong—so too do those dwelling in the forest flee, being afflicted by fear and tormented by dread.
Having obtained the true instruction and having seen the conviction regarding yoga, he inscribed [the realization that]:
"This perfection has been attained;
this perfection has been inscribed. This is the connection [of the meaning].

Having obtained the true instruction—that is, having received the teaching exactly as it is—and having seen the conviction regarding this yoga, that is, having observed the realization of this divine yoga, he dwells in the radiating pure knowledge; because its nature is radiant illumination, it is pure knowledge, and his dwelling is the state of the cessation of all afflictions.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining that [state], one should serve the lotus-feet of the Guru with hospitality,
according to the rules of giving, through physical austerities, and with prostrations.

Therefore, and for this very reason, in order to attain that [state] and to obtain its instruction, one should properly serve and worship the lotus-feet of the Guru who has received the signs [of realization]. This should be done with gentleness and goodwill, or by the rite of offering—such as the gift of excellent garments, prostrations with the body and hair, or in every possible way. Such worship of the Guru is the mother who gives birth to the supreme perfection of all knowledge; it is like a mother in this world to all beings. Whatever stainless merit I have thus acquired, bright as the rays of the full moon— [The remainder of the text follows: ...may that merit, which is pure and radiant as the light of the full moon, be for the benefit of all sentient beings. May it be for the welfare of all beings. May it be for the attainment of the state of omniscience. May it be for the destruction of the darkness of ignorance. May it be for the increase of the light of wisdom. May it be for the liberation from the ocean of saṃsāra. May it be for the attainment of the bliss of nirvāṇa. May it be for the fulfillment of the aspirations of all. May it be for the purification of all karmic obscurations. May it be for the realization of the ultimate truth. By that [merit], may all beings, having attained the noble mudrā which pacifies the fear of existence and accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings, become pure possessors of perfect enlightenment, free from the stains of the defilements of the age.

This concludes the *Svādhiṣṭhāna* [chapter], titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Reality" (*Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi*). May it be auspicious always! Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of reality" and so forth:

"Reality" (*tattva*) is non-arising (*anutpāda*). Thus, as stated in the *Jinajananī*: "That which is the non-arising of all phenomena is the Perfection of Wisdom. The accomplishment of the supreme knowledge of that reality is the "Accomplishment of the Supreme" (*Agra-siddhi*), the mother who gives birth to the wheel [of dharma], the mother who generates merit. Just as a mother in the world of the three realms (*traidhātuka*) gives birth to the desired objects for all sentient beings, she alone is merit (*puṇya*). It is wholesome (*kuśala*), free from faults (*doṣa*), and as radiant as the rays of the full moon.

By this merit, may all worlds be free from the stains of the Kali age; may they be devoid of the strife of the Kali age and the impurities of worldly afflictions. Having attained pure and perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and having reached the sublime Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) which pacifies the fear of existence—wherein "existence" (*bhava*) means *saṃsāra* and "peace" (*sama*) means *nirvāṇa*, thus it is that which pacifies both and wards off the grasping at them—it shall act for the benefit of all sentient beings and bring about the enlightenment of all beings.
Thus ends the "Method for the Dedication of Merit through Potency" in the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhiṭīkā*, composed by the monk Śrī Jñānacandra of moderate inclination.

Having meditated upon and contemplated the *cakramantra*—the mantra together with the wheel—the practitioner, by means of mental restraint through the speech of the heart, attains eight accomplishments (*siddhis*). These are: the accomplishment of collyrium, pills, sandals, medicinal herbs, jewels, mantras, yakṣa-women, and entry into another's body; the five higher knowledges (*abhijñās*), namely divine hearing, divine sight, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former births, and the supernormal power of movement; and likewise the eight qualities (*guṇas*): atomization (*aṇimā*), levitation (*laghimā*), expansion (*mahimā*), attainment (*iṣitva*), sovereignty (*vaśitva*), mastery (*kartṛtva*), subjugation (*bhojyatva*), and the fulfillment of every wish (*icchāprakāmajā*). These are the eight qualities. || 10 ||
He who meditates with effort every day at the four junctions of the day upon her whose face is radiant, and who is unconquerable even by Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha, conquers death.

The mantra practitioner who meditates with effort every day at the four junctions of the day— at dawn, midday, dusk, and midnight— upon Kiravaktrā, who has the face of a boar, shall conquer death in its embodied form, which is impossible for Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha to overcome.

For one who meditates upon the Aśanikola-mukhī with her wheel, there arise vast lands of clothing, food, drink, wealth, and grain, as well as palaces, divine beds, seats, and means of accomplishment; he also gains various beloved sciences.

Thus concludes the procedure for favoring disciples, along with its benefits, within the complete attainment of the knowledge of reality; "food" (*anna*) refers to eatable items, "clothing" (*vastra*) to garments, and "drink" (*pāna*) to milk and the like.

Wealth such as gold and the like, grain such as rice, vast lands, great earth, palaces, houses, divine beds such as mattresses, seats such as lion-thrones, and implements such as platforms—all these belong to that minister;

as do celestial women, various sciences, and manifold arts and crafts. This is for him who meditates upon Aśanikolamukhī, whose face is like a thunderbolt, together with her wheels—possessing two wheels above and below. ||12||
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Method for Benefiting Disciples along with its Benefits," in the *Ititatvajñānasaṃsiddhiṭīkā* composed by the monk Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Middle Way.

Now, therefore, the extraction of the mantra, which has come down through the lineage of gurus and constitutes the secret of the mantra, is being written down. Hereafter, I shall set forth the extraction of the mantra that is the heart of Vajrayoginī, which has been transmitted from ear to ear and from mouth to mouth in due succession. (1)
"Maṃtra," and so forth.

Hereafter, immediately following what was previously stated, I shall describe—that is, I will speak of—the extraction of the mantra (*maṃtrōddhāra*). It is the heart-essence of Vajrayoginī and the heart-essence of Kolamukhī, which has come from ear to ear, having been transmitted through a succession of ears, because it is held with the utmost reverence. || 1 ||

Having drawn a circle as previously described, one should then inscribe there, in regular order, the vowels and consonants (ālikāli) together with the abode of the hosts of Maruts, and likewise the corners.
As previously stated and as described before, one should draw the wheel in the form of the *dharmodayā*,

provided with the abode of the hosts of winds (*marudgaṇālaya*) and consisting of forty-nine squares; therein, one should inscribe the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*) in their proper sequence according to the prescribed order.
Starting from the letter A, there are sixteen.
